rv.q: There is not a safe moment, not a disposable emotion in this devastating, deeply felt revival.

The real surprise is that this 'Driving Miss Daisy' works as well as it does, and the reason why is that Ms. Tandy and Mr. Freeman have grown into their roles in ways that make their stage performances richer and more touching than what they did on screen.
This play has a timeless, soft appeal, even if some find it overly sentimental and corny.
Granted, you often wish the show bared more teeth instead of settling into comfortable, sepia-toned banter.

The result is that there is less dramatic impact in pivotal scenes like when Hoke, ordered by Miss Daisy to keep driving even though he has to go to the bathroom, finally rebels and asserts his independence.
Even “Driving Miss Daisy,” which opened on Monday night at the Golden Theater.
With three great actors -- Vanessa Redgrave, James Earl Jones and Boyd Gaines -- at their apogee, the enchanting revival of “Driving Miss Daisy” is the best theater can be.
'Daisy' finally makes it to theater's promised land with a dream team that's bound to strike fans as 'the second coming.'
So it shouldn't surprise that Jones' and Redgrave's performances here — by turns funny, tender, adorable and heartbreaking — rank with their best, most revelatory work.
Jones provides a congenial counterpart with an undercurrent of pain.
There's no apparent bond between these supposed best friends.
There are pleasures to be had, of course, and it's always instructive to watch the work of such consummate actors.
Best book your seats soon should you hope to witness these great artists give warm, winning life to the characters of starchy Atlanta matron Daisy Werthan and her devoted driver Hoke Coleburn.
The production is a tour de force for Vanessa Redgrave and James Earl Jones.
Jones gives a performance that I'd classify as one of the ten or so best I've ever seen in the theatre.

cn.t: Jones and Redgrave elevate Uhry's sentimental play with powerful, nuanced performances that critics hail as unmissable, though some find the material itself overly restrained and less effective than the film.
